The resulting quantum GEXIT function has area equal to the number of encoded qubits per channel use for any stabilizer code, and this applies to the depolarizing channel through its joint four-valued Pauli-error distribution. For CSS codes on the quantum erasure channel and under independent bit- and phase-flip noise, the logical correction problem separates into two binary coset-decoding problems. On the quantum erasure channel, the duality between the stabilizer group and the Pauli operators that commute with it gives a folding identity at complementary erasure probabilities. Using this and the area theorem, we derive an upper bound on the rate of code families with vanishing logical error probability that matches the capacity of the quantum erasure channel. For the depolarizing channel, we also derive a rate-dependent converse, using a connection between correction-class entropy and coherent information to establish an inequality involving the complementary channel.
item.dc:creator: Avijit Mandal, Mert G\"{o}kduman, Henry D. Pfister

item.title: Development of a fabrication-to-benchtop process for SiN-based quantum devices
item.description: arXiv:2610.22776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Silicon nitride has emerged as a key material for the advancement of future quantum communication and computational devices. However, challenges persist in establishing a comprehensive development process, spanning from fabrication to optical characterization, essential for advancing these devices to their next stage of potential. Maintaining control over the entire process, from start to finish, alongside device modeling, enables more efficient and timely iteration and optimization. Here we introduce a fabrication-to-benchtop process. We employ an in-house stoichiometric recipe for device fabrication and conduct comprehensive characterization of optical losses and material properties. Understanding and controlling the refractive index of the device are vital for predicting device geometries and group indices. Implementing the refractive indices of our fabricated devices, we simulate microring resonators and demonstrate their application in generating optical solitons.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE), Montreal, QC, Canada, 2024, pp. 699-70,
item.dc:creator: Connor Kupchak, Abubaker Tareki, Tara Moradi, Patrick Laferriere, Niall Tait, Khaled Mnaymneh

item.title: Chirality-resolved imaging of spin waves with a quantum spin
item.description: arXiv:2610.22867v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spin waves carry their propagation direction in the handedness of their circularly polarized stray field, a property inaccessible to scalar magnetometers. In the Damon-Eshbach surface wave of an in-plane magnetized film, the dipolar field above the film rotates with a handedness fixed by the direction of travel. The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre in diamond is an intrinsic polarization analyser: a right-handed field about the NV axis drives one spin transition, and a left-handed field drives the other, in both the ground and the excited state. Here, we exploit the two excited-state transitions, which lie inside the spin-wave band of yttrium iron garnet (YIG), as a pair of chirality channels and image Damon-Eshbach waves in both directions. Because reflection from an etched boundary reverses the handedness, the incident and reflected waves appear as two lines in one spectrum and are imaged separately. In the ground state, the same rule applies, and the selected field drives Rabi oscillations, a route to chirality-selective control of the NV spin by magnons. Reading the two channels gives the direction of a spin wave at one point, without a phase reference. This advances chirality-resolved quantum sensing and provides insight into chiral spin-wave dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Enbo Zhang, Tiancheng Zheng, Bo-Yuan Yang, Shreyes Nallan, Chengchao Xu, Mark Ku, Jian-Gang Zhu

item.title: Nonergodicity from Hilbert-Subspace Cloning
item.description: arXiv:2610.23105v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We identify a class of nonintegrable quantum many-body systems composed of single Pauli strings that possess an extensive number of noncommuting local conserved quantities and exhibit partial ergodicity breaking due to exponentially degenerate energy spectra. We show that such systems exhibit a novel mechanism, Hilbert-subspace cloning, where the identical chaotic Hamiltonian acts on each of exponentially many disconnected Hilbert subspaces. Although the dynamics within each clone thermalizes, quantum coherence between clones remains protected and detectable by local observables. Consequently, the long-time behavior of local observables is described by a coherence-preserving partial Gibbs ensemble, where the hidden subsystem retains its initial quantum coherence.
item.dc:creator: Yuuya Chiba, Ryusuke Hamazaki

item.title: From quantum emitters to technological platforms: a perspective on semiconductor quantum dots
item.description: arXiv:2610.23106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Photonic quantum technologies are based on controlled photon states. To generate these, quantum dots have emerged as excellent sources of single and entangled photons. In this Perspective, we briefly review the chronological development of quantum dots as photon sources, from their beginnings as quantum emitters in the early 2000s to the advanced photonic devices being developed today. We highlight the interplay between fundamental research and industrial aspects before discussing the photonic quantum technologies we expect to emerge in the near future.
item.dc:creator: Klaus D. J\"ons, Dorian A. Gangloff, Doris E. Reiter

item.title: Multiscale Quantum-Classical Simulation of Protein Autoproteolysis in a Million-Atom Membrane Environment
item.description: arXiv:2610.23108v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predicting chemical reactions in biomolecules is challenging because reactive centers are embedded within complex environments that strongly influence their energetics and mechanisms. Here, we present a hybrid quantum-classical workflow that combines molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and correlated wavefunction methods, tightly integrating CPUs, GPUs, and quantum processing units (QPUs) to enable simulations across multiple length and accuracy scales. We apply this approach to ADGRG1 autoproteolysis, a maturation reaction in an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor that has not previously been studied using correlated electronic-structure methods. Our simulations treat a biologically realistic system containing more than one million atoms, including the full-length uncleaved receptor embedded in an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane, while incorporating a 54-qubit IQM quantum processor and up to 1,200 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. These results demonstrate how quantum computers can serve as accelerators within scalable scientific workflows, extending correlated electronic-structure methods to biologically relevant systems.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Orlov, Alexis Ralli, Tim Weaving, Michael Williams de la Bastida, Reuben Martin, Zohim Chandani, Minh Chung, P. V. Sriluckshmy, Fedor Simkovic IV, Luigi Iapichino, Peter J. Love, Christian B. Mendl, Andrea Townsend-Nicholson, Peter V. Coveney

item.title: Unconditional Quantum PAC Learning Advantage in the Large Error Regime
item.description: arXiv:2610.23268v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish an unconditional super-polynomial separation between quantum and classical PAC learning of Boolean functions under the uniform distribution in the large error regime. For every advantage $\lambda(n) = n^{-\omega(1)}$, we construct a concept class that a polynomial-time quantum learner learns to agreement $1/2+\lambda(n)$ with success probability at least $1-1/n^k$. The learner uses only quantum random examples and outputs a polynomial-size deterministic classical circuit. In contrast, no polynomial-time classical learner achieves agreement $1/2 + \lambda(n)/n^k$ with success probability greater than $1/n^k$, even with membership queries. To achieve this, we develop a nearly-optimal quantum learner that uses quantum random examples to produce a hypothesis achieving a prescribed correlation with an arbitrary Boolean function. The learner generalizes Fourier sampling from parity hypotheses to quadratic hypotheses. While standard Fourier sampling is insensitive to the sign of the correlation, we use interference to bias sampling toward positively correlated hypotheses. This is combined with a careful analysis of the resulting distribution to boost both the learner's success probability and its agreement with the target function. We believe that the resulting quantum learning algorithm might be of independent interest. Finally, although a robust quantum PAC learning advantage holds unconditionally in the large error regime, we note that an analogous separation between quantum and classical learning in the small error regime would imply that $\mathsf{NP} \nsubseteq \mathsf{BPP}$.
item.dc:creator: Igor C. Oliveira

item.title: Action-Quantized Scar Multiplets and Dissipative Cat States from Fractal Period-Locking in the Open Quantum Baker Map
item.description: arXiv:2610.23573v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We open the quantum baker map with a position window of width $w$ and center $q_c$. Classical pruning tiles the $(q_c,w)$ plane into diamonds where the $T$ leading resonances form root-of-unity multiplets. At $w=1/2$ one periodic orbit survives for almost every $q_c$, and the multiplets are quantized without free parameters: their modulus $2^{-1/2}$ saturates the pressure bound and their phase is the orbit action. They form cycling multicomponent cat states, and the opening becomes one mid-circuit measurement, enabling spectroscopy with $\sim10^2$ shots on quantum processors.
item.dc:creator: Leonardo Ermann

item.title: Holographic two-point functions across a PT symmetry-breaking transition
item.description: arXiv:2610.23580v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In parity-time (PT)-symmetric non-Hermitian systems, an exceptional point, where eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce, typically separates a real spectrum from complex-conjugate eigenvalues. In logarithmic conformal field theories (LCFTs), such an exceptional point appears in the spectrum of scaling dimensions. Holographic models of LCFTs, such as the dipole model, are built exactly at this point. Here, we deform the holographic dipole model so that its two coalescing scaling dimensions split into either two real ones or a complex-conjugate pair. We obtain the renormalized two-point functions in closed form. They change continuously from a linear combination of two power laws, through the logarithmic form of the LCFT at the exceptional point, to log-periodic oscillations. For any pair of scalar primary operators with real mixing under dilatations, the conformal Ward identities fix this form up to two normalization constants, which the holographic dictionary determines. In PT-symmetric theories with such a dilatation operator, real and complex-conjugate scaling dimensions correspond to the PT-unbroken and PT-broken phases. In the BTZ black hole at finite temperature, the difference between the quasinormal frequencies associated with the two scaling dimensions changes from purely imaginary to purely real across the real-to-complex spectral transition. Correspondingly, the linear response changes from overdamped to underdamped, with critical damping at the exceptional point.
item.dc:creator: Zuo Wang, Liang He

item.title: Impact of Irrep Truncations on Quantum Simulations of QCD
item.description: arXiv:2610.23681v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories with continuous gauge groups require a choice of basis (how states of the gauge theory map to the qubit computational basis) and truncation scheme (which of the infinitely many gauge theory basis states should be omitted in the map to the finite dimensional qubit Hilbert space.) The most common choices are adapted to an electric basis for the gauge theory, where the basis states for each link are associated with irreducible representations of the gauge group. Electric bases and truncations are generally advantageous for preserving gauge symmetries and simulating the strong coupling regime, but their effectiveness in the weak coupling regimes of physical interest are less well understood. In this work, we compute relative probabilities $p(R')/p(R)$ for finding a link in the irreps $R,R'$ in the ground state of SU(3) lattice gauge theory using Euclidean Monte Carlo methods and weak-coupling lattice perturbation theory. The observables that compute these relative probabilities are constructed by introducing seams into an anisotropic lattice, and by a similar construction we are also able to measure relative probabilities of different site singlets (ways that electric flux braids together into a gauge singlet) at each vertex. With these methods we can quantify, for example, the importance of higher electric flux states in the weak coupling ground state. These results directly inform what truncations are needed to accurately capture non-abelian gauge dynamics near the continuum limit.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Draper, Drishti Gupta

item.title: Scaling of entanglement with distance between subsystems: detection of phase transitions in the $t'$-$\pi$-flux model
item.description: arXiv:2610.23770v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The system-size scaling of bipartite entanglement can be used to detect phase transitions. We develop a related approach for strongly correlated electron models where large density matrices or large system size scaling are inaccessible. To this end, we demonstrate that phase transitions of various kinds are signaled by a sharp signature in the first- or second-order logarithmic derivatives of the negativity measuring entanglement between small clusters at varying distances. Crucially, we show how to mitigate the effect of quantum Monte Carlo noise at large distances when computing the negativity. Our focus is on the $t'$-$\pi$-flux Hubbard model using auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations. It has the particular advantage of showing three distinct phase transitions in a single model: semimetal to band insulator, semimetal to antiferromagnetic Mott insulator, and a magnetic order-disorder transition belonging to the Gaussian, Gross-Neveu, and O(3) Wilson-Fisher universality classes, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Maksim Ulybyshev, Gerg\H{o} Ro\'osz, Gabriele Bellomia, Karsten Held, Fakher Assaad, Frederic Bippus

item.title: Transport and thermalization under noncommuting localized constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.23781v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the effects of spatially localized conserved quantities on transport and thermalization in quantum and classical many-body systems. We consider several related models: the integrable quantum Volterra model, its nonintegrable classical limit, and two cellular automata derived from the latter. Although localized constraints are often associated with lattice gauge theories, our models do not admit such an interpretation. In systems with discrete degrees of freedom, these constraints induce uniform fragmentation of the Hilbert or configuration space. In the quantum Volterra model, we derive an exact mapping of the dynamics within each Hilbert-space fragment onto a quantum chiral Potts chain. We find that energy transport is ballistic, with identical transport coefficients across all fragments. In the nonintegrable classical limit, energy transport is diffusive, and we similarly find the diffusion constant to be independent of whether or not the constraints are fixed (resolved). Finally, in the cellular automata, we show that, despite leaving transport unaffected, localized constraints lead to a strong breakdown of local ergodicity.
item.dc:creator: Amir Nesturov, Attila Tak\'acs, Lenart Zadnik

item.title: Experimental Demonstration of a Balanced Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifier
item.description: arXiv:2610.23810v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Superconducting travelling-wave parametric amplifiers (TWPAs) provide broadband gain, low added noise, and high dynamic range, making them attractive for applications requiring wide instantaneous bandwidth. This is crucial for amplifying multiplexed narrow band signals spread over a wide frequency range, such as qubit resonator arrays, or amplifying inherently wide band signals, such as in spectrometers or radiometers. In many cases, however, the useful bandwidth of a TWPA is limited by the production of the idler tone at an image frequency. For three-wave-mixing (3WM) TWPAs, for example, an input signal at $f_s$ is indistinguishable from one at $f_p - f_s$, which can produce spectral ambiguity when the input spectrum is broadband or not known in advance. We experimentally demonstrate a balanced architecture that doubles the instantaneous image-rejected bandwidth available to a 3WM TWPA by spatially separating the amplified signal from the output pump and generated idler, which resolves the sideband degeneracy. The architecture consists of two amplifiers connected between a pair of 180$^{\circ}$ hybrid couplers, with the signal and pump injected and output through the sum and difference ports, respectively. Using two kinetic-inductance TWPAs, we demonstrate approximately 20 dB of signal gain across nearly an octave of bandwidth, together with pump rejection below --20 dB and an average image rejection of approximately --15 dB over the operating band. These results establish balanced TWPAs as a practical approach to broadband parametric amplification, enabling improved contamination free bandwidth and eliminating the need for complex filtering.
item.dc:creator: Nikita Klimovich, Peter K. Day, Henry G. Leduc, Boon-Kok Tan

item.title: Anyonic Neural Network Wavefunctions
item.description: arXiv:2610.23815v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The macroscopic behavior of a non-interacting gas of Abelian anyons has remained unsettled for many decades. Prior numerical methods employing exact diagonalization in the continuum and on the plane have been limited to small system sizes, at most $N = 4$ anyons. Using the rapidly developing technology of neural network wavefunctions, we develop variational ansatze appropriate for studying continuum models of the Abelian anyon gas. The neural network architecture, which we call "AnyNet", is capable of exactly enforcing the non-analytic short-distance behavior induced by the anyonic statistics. We demonstrate excellent agreement with exact diagonalization for $N=4$ anyons, obtain accurate results up to $N = 16$ for intermediate statistics, and study up to $N=20$ for almost-fermionic anyons, matching perturbative results within a 0.4% discrepancy. We use this methodology to study anyons in a harmonic trap, and anyonic atoms as a model for anyon binding to impurities. We study the structure of anyonic wavefunctions as the statistics parameter is varied. We focus on the single-particle density, the pair density, the angular momentum, and the scaling of the wavefunction as multiple anyons coalesce. This work opens doors to understanding the macroscopic behavior of anyons, for which rich phases have been predicted theoretically.
item.dc:creator: Andres Perez Fadon, Pok Man Tam, Leyna Shackleton

item.title: MIP*=RE
item.description: arXiv:2001.04383v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that the class MIP* of languages that can be decided by a classical verifier interacting with multiple all-powerful quantum provers sharing entanglement is equal to the class RE of recursively enumerable languages. Our proof builds upon the quantum low-degree test of (Natarajan and Vidick, FOCS 2018) and the classical low-individual degree test of (Ji, et al., 2020) by integrating recent developments from (Natarajan and Wright, FOCS 2019) and combining them with the recursive compression framework of (Fitzsimons et al., STOC 2019). An immediate byproduct of our result is that there is an efficient reduction from the Halting Problem to the problem of deciding whether a two-player nonlocal game has entangled value $1$ or at most $1/2$. Using a known connection, undecidability of the entangled value implies a negative answer to Tsirelson's problem: we show, by providing an explicit example, that the closure $C_{qa}$ of the set of quantum tensor product correlations is strictly included in the set $C_{qc}$ of quantum commuting correlations. Following work of (Fritz, Rev. Math. Phys. 2012) and (Junge et al., J. Math. Phys. 2011) our results provide a refutation of Connes' embedding conjecture from the theory of von Neumann algebras.
item.dc:creator: Zhengfeng Ji, Anand Natarajan, Thomas Vidick, John Wright, Henry Yuen

item.title: Exponential clustering of bipartite quantum entanglement at arbitrary temperatures
item.description: arXiv:2108.12209v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Macroscopic quantum effects play central roles in the appearance of inexplicable phenomena in low-temperature quantum many-body physics. Such macroscopic quantumness is often evaluated using long-range entanglement, i.e., entanglement in the macroscopic length scale. The long-range entanglement not only characterizes the novel quantum phases but also serves as a critical resource for quantum computation. Thus, the problem that arises is under which conditions can the long-range entanglement be stable even at room temperatures. Here, we show that bi-partite long-range entanglement is unstable at arbitrary temperatures and exponentially decays with distance. Our theorem provides a no-go theorem on the existence of the long-range entanglement. The obtained results are consistent with the existing observations that long-range entanglement at non-zero temperatures can exist in topologically ordered phases, where tripartite correlations are dominant. In the derivation of our result, we introduce a quantum correlation defined by the convex roof of the standard correlation function. We establish an exponential clustering theorem for generic quantum many-body systems for such a quantum correlation at arbitrary temperatures, which yields our main result by relating quantum correlation to quantum entanglement. As a simple application of our analytical techniques, we derived a general limit on the Wigner-Yanase-Dyson skew information and the quantum Fisher information, which will attract significant attention in the field of quantum metrology. Our work reveals novel general aspects of low-temperature quantum physics and sheds light on the characterization of long-range entanglement.
item.dc:creator: Tomotaka Kuwahara, Keiji Saito

item.title: Molecular Ground State Simulation by Subspace Restriction and Hund's Rule
item.description: arXiv:2404.03268v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Subspace Restriction Scheme (SRS) is presented to address the qubit and resource constraints of molecular simulation on near-term quantum hardware. SRS restricts a molecular Hamiltonian to a selected determinant subspace before qubit encoding, so a $D$-dimensional subspace requires only $q=\lceil\log_2D\rceil$ qubits. We apply SRS to the established seniority-resolved Multi-Hund Subspaces $\mathrm{MHS}(\Omega)$ and develop compact encodings for these sectors. At fixed seniority and filling fraction, MHS asymptotically uses about half as many qubits as a compact particle-conserving encoding. For the $\mathrm{H}_{22}$ chain, the register shrinks from $44$ to $20$ qubits. Compression can nevertheless increase Pauli-operator density and does not always reduce measurement cost. In noiseless VQE benchmarks, shallow circuits reach within $1.6$~mHa of the exact subspace minima using only $4$--$30$ CNOT gates. However, the corresponding subspace minima for LiH, HF, OH, and CH remain $4.39$--$9.73$~mHa above FCI. Full-space UCCSD reaches chemical accuracy but requires hundreds to thousands of CNOT gates. SRS therefore provides a controlled resource--accuracy trade-off when register width is the binding constraint and the target state is well represented within a selected seniority sector.
item.dc:creator: Tsung-Chi Chiang, Calvin Ku, Jyh-Pin Chou, Alice Hu, Peng-Jen Chen, Ching-Jui Lai

item.title: Inverse Current in Coupled Transport: A Quantum Thermodynamic Model
item.description: arXiv:2405.01295v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The recent discovery of inverse current in coupled transport (ICC) in classical systems [Wang et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 110607 (2020)] -- where an induced current flows opposite to two mutually parallel thermodynamic forces, yet remains consistent with the second law of thermodynamics--reveals a striking and counterintuitive transport phenomenon. Using an exactly solvable model of strongly coupled quantum dots, we develop a thermodynamic framework to describe the ICC phenomenon at the quantum level. By systematically connecting the microscopic and macroscopic formulations of the entropy production rate in terms of appropriate entropic biases and entropic fluxes, our analysis identifies the conditions under which a genuine ICC effect can arise in quantum thermal transport and highlights potential applications in autonomous quantum engines and refrigerators.
item.dc:creator: Shuvadip Ghosh, Nikhil Gupt, Arnab Ghosh

item.title: Continuous variable dense coding under realistic non-ideal scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2407.07609v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We analyze the continuous variable (CV) dense coding protocol between a single sender and a single receiver when affected by noise in the shared and encoded states, as well as when the decoding is imperfect. We present a formalism to derive the dense coding capacity (DCC) of generic two-mode Gaussian states when affected by Gaussian noise models. When the constituent modes are affected by quantum-limited amplifiers, pure-loss channels, and environmental interactions, together with an inefficient decoding mechanism comprising imperfect double-homodyne detection, we specifically investigate the performance of the two-mode squeezed vacuum state (TMSV) by varying the strength of the noise. Through numerical simulations, we further show that the negative conditional entropy may be used to assess the quantum advantage of CV dense coding in Gaussian setups. While comparing the TMSV with other Gaussian states, we identify a class of pure Gaussian states capable of furnishing a capacity equal to that of the TMSV, under equal energy constraints in the ideal regime. Further, we demonstrate that, while the TMSV state is more susceptible to noise, it still provides the maximum quantum advantage in the DC protocol under practical conditions.
item.dc:creator: Mrinmoy Samanta, Ayan Patra, Rivu Gupta, Aditi Sen De

item.title: Bottlenecks in quantum channels and finite temperature phases of matter
item.description: arXiv:2412.09598v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove an analog of the "bottleneck theorem," well-known for classical Markov chains, for Markovian quantum channels. In particular, we show that if two regions (subspaces) of Hilbert space are separated by a region that has very low weight in the channel's steady state, then states initialized on one side of this barrier will take a long time to relax, putting a lower bound on the mixing time in terms of an appropriately defined "quantum bottleneck ratio." Importantly, this bottleneck ratio involves not only the probabilities of the relevant subspaces, but also the size of off-diagonal matrix elements between them. For low temperature quantum many-body systems, we use the bottleneck theorem to bound the performance of any quasilocal Gibbs sampler. This leads to a new perspective on thermally stable quantum phases in terms of a decomposition of the Gibbs state into multiple components separated by bottlenecks. As a concrete application, we show rigorously that weakly perturbed commuting projector models with extensive energy barriers (which include certain classical and quantum expander codes) have exponentially large mixing times
item.dc:creator: Tibor Rakovszky, Benedikt Placke, Nikolas P. Breuckmann, Vedika Khemani

item.title: Floquet-ADAPT-VQE: A Quantum Algorithm to Simulate Non-Equilibrium Physics in Periodically Driven Systems
item.description: arXiv:2503.11613v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit many fascinating phenomena absent in equilibrium systems, but their simulation is more challenging than that of static systems. Consequently, quantum simulation of these systems offers greater opportunity for achieving quantum advantage. To build the foundation for simulating time-periodic Hamiltonians, we utilize the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism to transform the Hamiltonian into a time-independent form and provide its Pauli decomposition. Within this formalism, we develop a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, Floquet-ADAPT-VQE, that produces three key quantities that govern periodically driven quantum dynamics: the quasienergy, the associated Floquet eigenstates, and expectation values of observables with respect to these eigenstates. The latter is achieved by applying a fixed-depth quantum circuit to an initial Floquet eigenstate---an efficient construction made possible by the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism. We also identify a suitable auxiliary initial state whose squared Floquet energy is independent of the number of auxiliary qubits as well as the driving frequency, which leads to better convergence with fewer ADAPT iterations. We demonstrate our algorithm by performing numerical simulations on a periodically driven XYZ model with a magnetic field. We also explore potential applications of our algorithm for studying various non-equilibrium phenomena in periodically driven systems.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Kumar, Karunya Shirali, Nicholas J. Mayhall, Sophia E. Economou, Edwin Barnes

item.title: Predicting Dynamics from Flows of the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis
item.description: arXiv:2504.01073v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Analytical treatments of far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics are few, even in well-thermalizing systems. The celebrated eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) provides a post hoc ansatz for the matrix elements of observables in the eigenbasis of a thermalizing Hamiltonian, given various response functions of those observables as input. However, the ETH cannot predict these response functions. We introduce a procedure, dubbed the statistical Jacobi approximation (SJA), to update the ETH ansatz after a perturbation to the Hamiltonian and predict perturbed response functions. The Jacobi algorithm diagonalizes the perturbation through a sequence of two-level rotations. The SJA implements these rotations statistically assuming the ETH throughout the diagonalization procedure, and generates integrodifferential flow equations for various form factors in the ETH ansatz. We approximately solve these flow equations using statistical information about Jacobi rotations as input, and predict both quench dynamics and autocorrelators in the thermal state of the perturbed Hamiltonian. The predicted dynamics agree with exact numerics in both random matrix models and spin chains, outperforming second-order time-dependent perturbation theory.
item.dc:creator: Dominik Hahn, David M. Long, Marin Bukov, Anushya Chandran

item.title: Characterization of Linear Measurements in Cavity Optomechanics: Examples and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2508.21419v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Detailed understanding of physical measurements is essential for devising efficient metrological strategies and measurement-feedback schemes, as well as finding fundamental limitations on measurement sensitivity. In the quantum regime, measurements modify the state of the system of interest through measurement backaction as a direct consequence of the Heisenberg principle. In cavity optomechanics and electromechanics, a plethora of strategies exist for measuring the mechanical motion using electromagnetic fields, each leading to different competition between measurement imprecision and backaction. While this range of techniques allows broad applications of optomechanical and electromechanical devices, it makes direct comparison of different measurement methods difficult. We develop a formalism for quantifying the performance of optomechanical measurements using a few relevant figures of merit. Our approach is inspired by similar characterizations in quantum optics and quantifies the main properties of quantum measurements -- the ability to distinguish different quantum states and preservation of signal in the presence of measurement noise. We demonstrate our concept on the most common optomechanical measurements -- displacement detection, coherent quantum noise cancellation, and quantum nondemolition measurements -- and perform detailed analysis of errors in optomechanical nondemolition measurements. This newly acquired knowledge allows us to propose a strategy for quantum nondemolition measurements in levitodynamics using coherent scattering. Our results complement existing knowledge of linear optomechanical interactions and open the way to new understanding of optomechanical measurements, thus allowing also novel applications of optomechanical devices in fundamental physics and quantum technologies.
item.dc:creator: F. Bemani, O. \v{C}ernot\'ik, R. Filip

item.title: Diagrammatic Reasoning with Control as a Constructor, Applications to Quantum Circuits
item.description: arXiv:2508.21756v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Control is a fundamental concept in quantum and reversible computational models. It enables the conditional application of a transformation to a system, depending on the state of another system. We introduce a general framework for diagrammatic reasoning featuring control as a constructor. To this end, we provide an elementary axiomatization of control functors, extending the standard formalism of PROPs to controlled PROPs. As an application, we show that controlled PROPs facilitate diagrammatic reasoning for quantum circuits by introducing a simple and complete set of relations involving at most three qubits, whereas in the standard PROP setting any complete axiomatization necessarily requires relations acting on arbitrarily many qubits.
item.dc:creator: No\'e Delorme, Simon Perdrix

item.title: Circuit-based characterization of finite-temperature quantum phases and self-correcting quantum memory
item.description: arXiv:2509.15204v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum phases at zero temperature can be characterized as equivalence classes under local unitary transformations: two ground states within a gapped phase can be transformed into each other via a local unitary circuit. We generalize this circuit-based characterization of phases to systems at finite-temperature thermal equilibrium described by Gibbs states. We construct a channel circuit that approximately transforms one Gibbs state into another provided the two are connected by a path in parameter space along which a certain correlation-decay condition holds. For finite-dimensional systems of linear size $L$ and approximation error $\epsilon$, the locality of the circuit is ${\rm polylog}({\rm poly}(L)/\epsilon)$. The correlation-decay condition, which we specify, is expected to be satisfied in the interior of many noncritical thermal phases, including those displaying discrete symmetry breaking and topological order. As an application, we show that any system in the same thermal phase as a zero-temperature topological code coherently preserves quantum information for a macroscopically long time, establishing self-correction as a universal property of thermal phases. As part of the proof, we provide explicit encoding and decoding channel circuits to encode information into, and decode it from, a system in thermal equilibrium.
item.dc:creator: Ruochen Ma, Vedika Khemani, Shengqi Sang

item.title: Phase-preserving steady-state operations beyond Lindblad master equations
item.description: arXiv:2510.10394v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider a class of nonunitary operations that is naturally implemented via a combination of projective measurement and unitary operators. We implement these operations without using measurements by coupling the system to an infinite set of ancilla states and time-evolving with a single time-independent Hamiltonian. The infinite ancilla enables the main system to reach a local steady state that preserves initial phase information. We prove that these steady-state operations are not describable as a mapping from an initial state to a steady state of a time-independent Lindblad master equation acting only on the main system. As an additional degree of control, we show that the spectral resonance between the system and the ancilla acts as a switch that turns the operation on and off, and we derive a closed-form expression that quantifies the sharpness of this switch. We further find numerically that the phase preservation survives moderate disorder, over a time window set by the size of the ancilla. This Hamiltonian framework therefore provides a route to autonomous quantum control using the tunability of a closed system.
item.dc:creator: Man Yin Cheung, Mona Berciu, Kyle Monkman

item.title: Hybrid boson sampling-neural network architecture for enhanced classification
item.description: arXiv:2510.13332v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Demonstration of quantum advantage for classical machine learning tasks remains a central goal for quantum technologies and artificial intelligence. Two major bottlenecks to this goal are the high dimensionality of practical datasets and the limited performance of near-term quantum computers. Boson sampling is among the few models for which experiments have claimed quantum advantage, yet it has limited practical applications. Here, we propose a hybrid framework that combines the computational power of boson sampling with the adaptability of neural networks to construct quantum kernels that enhance support vector machine classification. The neural network adapts the data features onto a programmable boson sampling circuit, producing quantum states that span a high-dimensional Hilbert space and enable improved classification performance. Using four datasets with various classes, we demonstrate that our model outperforms classical linear and sigmoid kernels. These results highlight the potential of boson sampling-based quantum kernels for practical quantum-enhanced machine learning.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Sharifian, Abolfazl Bayat

item.title: The three kinds of three-qubit entanglement
item.description: arXiv:2511.07617v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We construct an important missing piece in the entanglement theory of pure three-qubit states, which is a polynomial measure of W-entanglement. This works in parallel to the three-tangle, which is a polynomial measure of GHZ-entanglement, and to the bipartite concurrence, which is a polynomial measure of bipartite entanglement. We also show that these entanglement measures are ordered, the bipartite measure is larger than the W measure, which is larger than the GHZ measure. It is meaningful then to consider these three types of three-qubit entanglement, which are also ordered, bipartite is weaker than W, which is weaker than GHZ, in parallel to the order of the three kinds of equivalence classes of entangled three-qubit states.
item.dc:creator: Szil\'ard Szalay

item.title: Higher-Dimensional Information Lattice: Quantum State Characterization through Inclusion-Exclusion Local Information
item.description: arXiv:2512.20793v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Developing a local description of quantum information is a central problem in quantum many-body physics: the goal is to identify how correlations are organized across positions and scales without choosing specific observables. We introduce a higher-dimensional information lattice, an inclusion-exclusion construction that decomposes the von Neumann information of reduced density matrices into contributions labeled by subsystem position and scale. Above one dimension, overlapping subsystems can form loops, allowing information associated with one subsystem to be inferred nonlocally from the density matrices of others. The sign of the inclusion-exclusion information resolves such overlap redundancies in position and scale: positive values mark positions and scales with net information gain, while negative values occur where redundant contributions dominate new ones. We implement the construction in two dimensions and apply it to many-body ground states with distinct entanglement structures. For localized states, such as disordered-localized states or gapped ground states of local Hamiltonians, the local information decays exponentially along different directions, defining direction-dependent information length scales. In critical states with a Fermi surface, decay becomes algebraic, with dominant directions tied to the velocity of gapless modes. In the toric code, topological order manifests as a negative information value at the largest lattice scale, interpreted as global information redundancy between the smallest loop-enclosing overlapping subsystems. We also isolate the universal information carried by edge states and locate the signatures of non-Abelian fusion channels in position and scale. Our results establish the higher-dimensional information lattice as a framework for resolving universal correlation structures through the spatial and scale distribution of quantum information.
item.dc:creator: Ian Matthias Fl\'or, Claudia Artiaco, Thomas Klein Kvorning, Jens H. Bardarson

item.title: Failure of the mean-field Hartree approximation for a bosonic many-body system with non-Hermitian Hamiltonian
item.description: arXiv:2601.13038v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mean-field Hartree theory is a central tool for reducing many-body dynamics to an effective one-particle evolution. This approximation has been employed when the Hamiltonian governing the many-body dynamics is not Hermitian. Indeed, non-Hermitian Hamiltonians model particle gain/loss or the evolution of open quantum systems between consecutive quantum jumps. Furthermore, the validity of the Hartree approximation for generic non-Hermitian Hamiltonians lies at the basis of a quantum algorithm for nonlinear differential equations. In this work, we show that this approximation can fail. First, we consider the most general bosonic mean-field Hamiltonian with two-body interactions and we prove that, for non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, the Hartree equation does not capture the correct second time derivative of the one-particle marginal state at $t=0$ in the thermodynamic limit. Then, we analytically solve a model of $N$ bosonic qubits with a purely anti-Hermitian Hamiltonian, compute the limit for $N\to\infty$ of the one-particle marginal state and show that it does not agree with the solution of the non-Hermitian Hartree equation. We further show that there exists an initial condition such that the exact one-particle marginal state undergoes a finite-time transition to a mixed state, a phenomenon that is completely absent in the case of Hermitian Hamiltonians. Finally, we simulate a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian with real spectrum and show that, also in this case, there are initial conditions for which the Hartree equation does not reproduce the correct one-particle marginal state in the limit $N\to\infty$. Our findings challenge the validity of the mean-field Hartree approximation for non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, and call for additional conditions for the validity of the mean-field regime to model the dynamics of particle gain and loss and the open-system dynamics in bosonic many-body systems.
item.dc:creator: Matias Ginzburg, Simone Rademacher, Giacomo De Palma

item.title: Low-Resource Quantum Energy Gap Estimation via Randomization
item.description: arXiv:2601.13881v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Estimating the energy spectra of quantum many-body systems is a fundamental task in quantum physics, with applications ranging from chemistry to condensed matter. Algorithmic shadow spectroscopy is a recent method that leverages randomized measurements on time-evolved quantum states to extract spectral information. However, implementing accurate time evolution with low-depth circuits remains a key challenge for near-term quantum hardware. In this work, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical protocol that integrates Time Evolution via Probabilistic Angle Interpolation (TE-PAI) into the shadow spectroscopy framework. TE-PAI enables the simulation of time evolution using shallow stochastic circuits while preserving unbiased estimates through quasiprobability sampling. We construct the combined estimator and derive its theoretical properties. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that our method accurately resolves energy gaps and exhibits enhanced robustness to gate noise compared to first-order Trotter-based shadow spectroscopy. We further validate the protocol experimentally on up to 20 qubits using IBM quantum hardware. This makes TE-PAI shadow spectroscopy a promising tool for spectral analysis on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Pages, Chusei Kiumi, Yuto Morohoshi, B\'alint Koczor, Kosuke Mitarai

item.title: Analytic formulae for non-local nonstabiliserness in bipartite systems of qutrits and ququints
item.description: arXiv:2603.09155v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We conjecture analytic expressions for the non-local magic of bipartite pure qudit states of prime local dimension. Our construction relies on the Schmidt-aligned state attaining the minimum over local unitaries, a hypothesis that we support with numerical evidence for pairs of qutrits and ququints. For composite local dimensions, we find that the analogous expressions do not in general reproduce the global minimum, but can still provide computationally cheap approximations to the non-local magic. We also find that relations between non-local magic and entanglement diagnostics that hold for two qubits generally do not extend to qutrit and higher-dimensional systems. As a few-body application, we evaluate the qutrit non-local magic generated by elastic pion scattering, treating hadronic isospin as the qutrit. We find that $p$-wave charged pion scattering realises the maximum non-local magic allowed in the system just below the $\rho$-meson resonance.
item.dc:creator: Giorgio Busoni, John Gargalionis, Ewan N. V. Wallace, Martin J. White

item.title: Analysis of Hydrogen Contamination in Al/AlOx/Al Josephson Junctions
item.description: arXiv:2603.14113v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hydrogen contamination in Josephson junctions may contribute to device-to-device variability in superconducting qubits, yet its incorporation, location, and bonding in tunnel barriers remain poorly understood. We combine molecular dynamics simulations of aluminum oxidation in dense O2 and H2O environments with atomistic quantum transport calculations. The simulations produce amorphous AlOx barriers with experimentally relevant hydrogen concentrations. Analysis of 400 statistically independent samples shows that the number of incorporated H atoms follows a beta-binomial distribution, reflecting correlations arising from self-limiting oxidation. Most H atoms reside near the AlOx surface, primarily in Al-OH and Al-OH-Al motifs. Quantum transport calculations for Al/Al2O3/Al junctions reveal that hydrogen enhances transmission near the Fermi level by creating an interface dipole that shifts the oxide bands relative to the electrode Fermi level. Combining hydrogen-number statistics with calculated transmission coefficients yields a probability distribution for the Josephson energy. At an average hydrogen content of 2.56 at.%, we predict E_J/h = 10.23 GHz with a standard deviation of 3.6 MHz. Hydrogen shifts the mean Josephson energy by approximately 11%, proportionally to its concentration, but contributes far less to device-to-device variability than observed in state-of-the-art fabricated junctions. These findings provide an atomistic understanding of hydrogen incorporation and its impact on Josephson energy.
item.dc:creator: Yu Zhu, Aldilene Saraiva-Souza, F\'elix Beaudoin, Hong Guo

item.title: Logarithmic-depth quantum state preparation of polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2603.16527v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum state preparation is a central primitive in many quantum algorithms, yet it is generally resource intensive, with efficient constructions known only for structured families of states. This work introduces a method for preparing quantum states whose amplitudes are given by a degree$-d$ polynomial, using circuits with logarithmic depth in the number $n$ of qubits and only $\mathcal O(n)$ ancilla qubits, improving previous approaches that required linear-depth circuits. The construction first relies on a block-encoding of an affine diagonal operator based on its Pauli-basis decomposition, which involves only $n$ terms. A modified linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) technique is introduced to implement this decomposition in logarithmic depth, together with a novel circuit for the EXACT-one oracle that flags basis states in which exactly one qubit is in the state $|1\rangle$. It then uses a generalized quantum eigenvalue transformation (GQET) to promote this affine operator to an arbitrary degree polynomial. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations are reported along with a proof-of-principle implementation on a trapped-ion quantum processor using $14$ qubits and more than $500$ primitive quantum gates. Because polynomial approximations are ubiquitous in scientific computing, this construction provides a scalable and resource-efficient approach to quantum state preparation, further improving the potential of quantum algorithms in fields such as chemistry, physics, engineering, and finance.
item.dc:creator: Baptiste Claudon, Alexis Lucas, Jean-Philip Piquemal, C\'esar Feniou, Julien Zylberman

item.title: Risk-aware neural pulse compilation of continuously parameterized single-qubit gates with optimal-control benchmarking and NMR hardware validation
item.description: arXiv:2604.11314v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pulse-level compilation can reduce the depth and calibration overhead associated with decomposing continuously parameterized quantum operations into fixed gate libraries, but conventional optimal control requires a new optimization for each target and can be sensitive to hardware uncertainty. We introduce a physics-informed neural compilation framework that learns a reusable map from continuously parameterized single-qubit gate targets directly to experimentally admissible control waveforms. The compiler is trained end-to-end through differentiable quantum dynamics without precomputed optimal-pulse labels, and its robustness is improved by first diagnosing physically relevant failure modes and then applying tail-risk-aware fine-tuning. On a three-qubit liquid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) model, the learned compiler generalizes across Haar-distributed single-qubit targets with mean nominal fidelity above 0.99 and generates new pulses in submillisecond inference time. Matched benchmarks reveal complementary advantages: robust gradient ascent pulse engineering (GRAPE) achieves the highest per-target fidelity, whereas the trained neural compiler amortizes the optimization cost across the target family, enabling substantially faster online pulse generation. Risk-aware training substantially broadens tolerance to radio-frequency (RF)-amplitude errors, including perturbations beyond the training range. Experiments on a three-spin NMR processor reproduce the predicted broadening of the RF-tolerance response, although the absolute experimental correlations are lower than the simulated values. These results establish a general workflow combining amortized machine learning, physical sensitivity diagnosis, risk-aware control, optimal-control benchmarking, and hardware testing, providing a route toward fast and robust pulse-level compilation for repeatedly varying quantum operations.
item.dc:creator: Arash Fath Lipaei, Ebrahim Khaleghian, Gani G\"oral, Zidong Lin, Selin Aslan, \"Ozg\"ur E. M\"ustecapl{\i}o\u{g}lu

item.title: Quantum instanton theory for metastable collective spin systems
item.description: arXiv:2604.15091v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Collective spin systems -- driven-dissipative spin ensembles whose unitary and dissipative processes act uniformly on all spins, allowing their dynamics to be described as a single macrospin -- play an important role in atomic and solid-state physics. Their intrinsic nonlinearity gives rise to multiple long-lived metastable states that ultimately relax to a unique most probable state. This dominant state can change with a control parameter, leading to first-order phase transitions. We develop a real-time instanton approach based on quantum quasiprobability dynamics that captures the stationary state in the large-spin limit and the asymptotic scaling of relaxation rates. We further show that these features are not accurately described by the previously applied semiclassical Wigner approach due to its neglect of non-Gaussian fluctuations.
item.dc:creator: Krzysztof Ptaszynski, Maciej Chudak, Massimiliano Esposito

item.title: Probability distribution analysis of the cascaded variational quantum eigensolver
item.description: arXiv:2605.00807v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The cascaded variational quantum eigensolver (CVQE) circumvents the need for iterative communication between the quantum and classical processing units that is necessary in the conventional VQE algorithm. While CVQE offers complete freedom to choose the guiding state as input, not all guiding states provide both accurate solutions and efficient resource usage. Our work presents a process based on trapezoidal-state preparation for selecting guiding states that yield accurate many-electron ground-state solutions with minimal resource consumption. By analyzing state probability distributions at different stages of CVQE calculations for the collision complex mediating the $\mathrm{H}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2^+ \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_3^+ + \mathrm{H}$ bimolecular reaction, we identify stage-specific errors, trace their impact on final classical optimization, and determine the optimal guiding-state parameters for given resource constraints. Our findings uncover a critical trade-off on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, demonstrating that shallower diabatic circuits provide the best compromise among optimization efficiency, state quality, sampling cost, and signal-to-noise ratio in our system.
item.dc:creator: Yi-Hua Lai, John P. T. Stenger, Gloria Bazargan, Igor V. Schweigert, Daniel Gunlycke

item.title: Separability from Multipartite Measures
item.description: arXiv:2605.02097v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that multi-invariants provide necessary and sufficient criteria for full separability in finite-dimensional multipartite systems. For tripartite three-qubit states, the third-order negativity gives an exact criterion for full separability for both pure and mixed states. We then extend the framework to four-qubit pure states, whose full characterization requires eighteen independent real parameters. We identify eighteen independent entanglement measures, consisting of six bipartite, eight tripartite, and four quadripartite measures, with the third-order negativity serving as a key separability criterion. Finally, we generalize the construction to multipartite qudit systems and discuss an application to conformal field theory.
item.dc:creator: Chen-Te Ma, Ma-Ke Yuan

item.title: Caustics and catastrophes in strong-field physics $-$ Picard-Lefschetz theory as a universal approach to saddle-point methods in attosecond science
item.description: arXiv:2605.03794v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ultrashort laser pulses on the attosecond timescale are typically achieved via high-order harmonic generation (HHG), a nonlinear process in which atoms interact with intense light fields to emit a broad spectrum of harmonics. HHG is commonly described in terms of a `quantum orbits' model based on several interfering electron trajectories, thereby incorporating both quantum-mechanical effects and an intuitive picture of classical dynamics. By tuning the parameters of the driving laser field, the interplay between these trajectories can be controlled, shaping the emitted light. Mathematically, this model expresses the harmonic response as a highly oscillatory integral. Applying saddle-point methods to this integral allows it to be decomposed into contributions from distinct saddle points of the semi-classical action, thereby linking quantum dynamics to classical trajectories. However, a general framework for applying these methods across arbitrary parameters and laser configurations has been missing. In this thesis, we introduce Picard-Lefschetz theory and develop practical numerical methods for its application. These enable the evaluation of oscillatory integrals and identification of contributions from individual critical points. We apply these techniques to strong-field ionisation and HHG, focusing on caustics $-$ enhancement features where trajectories coalesce and standard approximations fail. Our methods remain valid in these regions, allowing systematic analysis of parameter regimes and revealing previously inaccessible features. This work improves the understanding and control of ultrafast light-matter interactions.
item.dc:creator: Anne Weber

item.title: A finite-shot mean-squared-error boundary for Richardson zero-noise extrapolation
item.description: arXiv:2605.08251v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) reduces the bias of noisy quantum-circuit measurements, but Richardson coefficients and shot splitting increase their statistical error. This paper determines the noise strength at which Richardson ZNE starts to lower the mean-squared error relative to the unmitigated estimator at a fixed shot budget $B$. The boundary is set by the balance between the leading squared-bias improvement and the leading excess-variance penalty: depending on the variance exponent of the measurement, it shrinks with $B$, becomes a budget threshold, or disappears. For fixed Richardson extrapolation with linear leading bias, the Richardson order and the shot allocation change only constants; the boundary exponent is set by the measured observable and protocol. Deterministic stabilizer measurements and nonzero-variance Hamiltonian or variational-energy measurements have boundaries that shrink as $B^{-1}$ and $B^{-1/2}$, and for finite-outcome shot measurements these two classes are the only ones. Qiskit Aer simulations of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) and quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) circuits reproduce this separation, and on IBM Quantum hardware ZNE lowers the mean-squared error at equal budget in 75 of 101 instances.
item.dc:creator: Vicenzo Scavino Alfaro

item.title: Learning Midcircuit Measurement Backaction from Three Repeated Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2606.00433v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate modeling of midcircuit measurements (MCMs) is essential for dynamic-circuit operations such as syndrome extraction, measurement-based reset, and the separation of state-preparation and measurement error. Unlike terminal measurement, a noisy MCM both produces a classical outcome and alters the incoming quantum state, thereby influencing subsequent circuit operations. This makes conventional confusion-matrix or fidelity-level characterization insufficient. Here, we introduce an efficient, self-consistent protocol for learning a single-qubit Z-twirled MCM instrument, retaining the readout-backaction correlations and excitation-decay asymmetry that are erased in Pauli-error descriptions. Remarkably, readout bit strings from only three repeated MCMs on a maximally mixed input determine all learnable parameters of the reduced instrument, up to a single unidentifiable gauge degree of freedom. Physicality constraints convert this nonidentifiability into narrow, gauge-aware error intervals. Implemented on IBM superconducting processors, the learned instrument improves Pauli-observable prediction by $\sim 100\times$ over a conventional confusion-matrix model and reveals a $T_1$-decay dominated backaction. Our protocol provides a compact characterization layer for state-preparation and measurement error separation, reset optimization, and noise-aware quantum error correction.
item.dc:creator: Chia-Tung Chu, Su-un Lee, Han Zheng, Senrui Chen, Bibek Pokharel, Alireza Seif, Liang Jiang

item.title: Spectral theory of energy-selective quantum search with Ising Hamiltonian phase oracles
item.description: arXiv:2606.03380v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop an exact spectral-response theory for the Grover-type iterate \(W_T=D_\xi\exp(-\mathrm{i} T H)\), in which the evolution generated by a diagonal Ising Hamiltonian is used directly as a continuous phase oracle. An energy-grouped recurrence and its generating-function solution show how the empirical characteristic function determines the position, width, height, and saturation time of an energy-selective resonance. For an annealed Gaussian density of states, a high-density-tail resonance containing \(M\) configurations is reached after \(\Theta(\sqrt{2^n/M})\) oracle calls with success probability \(\Theta(1)\), giving a quadratic query improvement over independent uniform sampling with classical energy evaluation. For correlated random Ising spectra, overlap-dependent covariances lead to a realization-dependent resonance shift with root-mean-square scale \(O(n^{-3})\), parametrically larger than the resonance width, and can also reduce the peak height. The shift is both an algorithmic detuning and a coherent probe of sample-specific spectral fluctuations whose ensemble statistics reflect the Ising overlap structure. Spectral symmetrization and iterative calibration can remove or compensate the resonance-center displacement for prescribed-energy targeting. We also clarify the relation to designed spectral filters and the precision and coherence requirements of this asymptotic primitive.
item.dc:creator: A. S. Plyashechnik, A. A. Zhukov, A. V. Lebedev, W. V. Pogosov

item.title: Dominant Eigenstate Isolation through Symmetry-Orbit Decoupling
item.description: arXiv:2606.21962v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We address the problem of extracting a target eigenstate from an approximate pure state. Our approach, symmetry-orbit decoupling, exploits symmetries that preserve the target state while acting differently on the residual. Averaging over the resulting orbit suppresses the target--residual coherence without reducing the target population, thereby exposing a spectral structure that is hidden in the original pure state. When the target is sufficiently separated from the residual modes, it becomes the principal mode of the orbit-averaged state and can be identified through the orbit Gram matrix. Numerical VQE simulations performed with QuESTlink for six- and eight-qubit Heisenberg and Fermi--Hubbard chains show substantial improvements in ground-state energy estimation. The remaining accuracy is limited by residual components that are indistinguishable from the target under the chosen symmetry.
item.dc:creator: Canyu He, Chunhua Zeng, Ruyu Yang, Yongdan Yang

item.title: Enhancing Quantum Metrology with High-order Fisher Information and Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2606.27633v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fisher information plays a central role in statistics and quantum metrology, providing the basis for the celebrated Cram\'{e}r-Rao bound. In this work, we introduce a new information measure based on higher-order Fisher information and show that it naturally leads to a generalized uncertainty relation for parameter estimation, which can be regarded as an extension of the Cram\'er-Rao bound. As an application, we analyze the case of quantum phase estimation with a single qubit and compare our theoretical bounds with the well-known established hierarchical bounds. Finally, we experimentally validate the proposed framework using a photonic platform.
item.dc:creator: Xin-Zhu Liu, Jun-Li Jiang, Yan-Han Yang, Li-Ming Zhao, Xue Yang, Shao-Ming Fei, Ming-Xing Luo

item.title: Noise structuring in fixed-depth Trotter simulation: stationary channels and observable-level depolarization
item.description: arXiv:2607.17936v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We analyze fixed-depth Trotter simulation as a method for structuring hardware noise in digital many-body dynamics. The number of layers is chosen using the largest endpoint time and is then kept fixed throughout the time scan, making the total noise dose approximately independent of the endpoint time. For local stochastic faults, we show that, once propagated faults lose memory of their insertion layer, the noisy circuit factorizes into ideal evolution followed by a stationary finite-depth binomial channel. In the dilute-layer limit, this channel reduces to a Poissonian exponential. The memory time of a single fault is related to a Loschmidt echo. An important consequence is observable-level depolarization: for selected macroscopic observables at low to moderate noise levels, the stationary channel can act as an almost time-independent affine contrast correction, even though the full channel need not be depolarizing, which is crusial for error mitigation purposes. At short times, the same protocol produces a digital Zeno-like transient, in which a fixed number of noise opportunities competes with a vanishing coherent angle per layer. Our results also reveal limitations of naive zero-noise extrapolatin strategies based on oversimplified functions.
item.dc:creator: G. L. Stavisskii, W. V. Pogosov, L. E. Fedichkin, A. V. Lebedev

item.title: Quantum key distribution over a 2 km free-space channel with a high secure key rate
item.description: arXiv:2607.24118v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) provides crucial advantages, including mobility and deployment exibility, for securing next-generation communication networks. However, atmospheric turbulence and beam wander severely degrade single-photon coupling effciency and link stability over outdoor channels. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate a free-space decoy-state BB84 QKD system operating at 803 nm with a 100 MHz repetition rate over a 2 km outdoor link. By employing an active beam-wander correction based on fast-steering mirrors (FSMs) and position sensitive detectors (PSDs) with a 500 Hz control loop, we enhance the ?ber coupling effciency and achieve an average ?nite-key secure key rate of 110 kbps with an average quantum bit error rate (QBER) of 3.28 %, representing a 2.5 times secure key rate enhancement under an active beam stabilization. This work demonstrates the indispensability of active beam stabilization and provides an operational reference for robust, long-range free-space quantum communication.
item.dc:creator: Kyungdeuk Park, Dongkyu Kim, Dong-Gil Im, Yonggi Jo, Jisu Kim, Jonguk Choi, Yong Sup Ihn

item.title: Efficient LLM-Generated Shuttling Compilers for Complex Trapped-Ion Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2607.24714v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers rely on shuttling compilers, which cast an input algorithm into a sequence of ion-qubit movements within a given architecture. We present the first study in which a single frontier large language model (LLM), Claude Opus 4.7, generates and iteratively refines the Python code of shuttling compilers from written specifications. Starting with a compiler for (i) a linear segmented trap, we extend it to (ii) a trap with junctions, and finally achieve efficient compilation for (iii) a broad class of connected trap graphs. The compilers for the more general cases are seeded with code from the previous ones. We benchmark the LLM-generated compilers against state-of-the-art hand-crafted ones using a common suite of quantum circuits. The number of shuttling timesteps is reduced by up to 72% for (i) and up to 43% for (ii). For the broad case (iii) of freely connected architectures, we find large variations in the required number of shuttling timesteps, depending on the connectivity. A densely connected, junction-rich architecture yields up to an order-of-magnitude reduction in shuttling timesteps compared to a corridor-like one. Repeating the complete generation and evaluation with a second frontier LLM, Claude Fable 5, reproduces these findings, with the Fable 5 compilers surpassing the hand-crafted ones more often on the largest circuits. Our results show that an unmodified frontier LLM can produce working, correct, and competitive shuttling compilers without additional manual algorithmic engineering. Generating compilers this way reduces the development time for new architectures from several months to a few days.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Kreppel, Reza Salkhordeh, Ferdinand Schmidt-Kaler, Andr\'e Brinkmann

item.title: Exact minimum measurement dependence for faithful local deterministic models of multipartite GHZ-Mermin correlations
item.description: arXiv:2608.00124v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A local deterministic model can reproduce Bell-inequality violations only if the hidden state depends on the measurement settings. Hall found the minimum such dependence for the singlet state [Phys. Rev. Lett. 105, 250404 (2010)] and posed the corresponding problem for the Mermin state [Phys. Rev. A 84, 022102 (2011)]. This paper solves it, for the $n$-party GHZ-Mermin scenario at every $n \geq 3$, with the marginals reproduced as well as the correlators. The minimum measurement-dependence fraction is $F_{\min}(n) = R/[2(R+1)]$, with $R = 2^{\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor}$ the Mermin violation ratio: $1/3, 2/5, 4/9, 8/17, \ldots$, always below $1/2$. The lower bound follows from Mermin's inequality by a general overlap bound; the upper bound is an explicit model, uniform on the hidden-variable classes that violate the fewest constraints, with closed-form counts; a reduction theorem shows that for Mermin scenarios the marginals impose no additional dependence. The Mermin values are also certified by integer-arithmetic enumeration through $n = 22$. Every minimal contradiction of size $k$ among stabilizer constraints has correlator-only minimum $1/(k-1)$. With the marginals included the minimum is the same on every core of the $C_5$ ring cluster, on the size-4 and size-5 cores of $C_4$ and on every four-core of $C_6$, but larger on the size-6 and size-7 cores of $C_4$ and on 112 of the 1,920 five-cores of $C_6$, with exact certificates on both sides in every case.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Alai

item.title: A Quantum Roadmap for Softmax Attention: Exact Born-Rule Analogs for Softmax Attention on the Probability Simplex
item.description: arXiv:2608.11173v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The attention mechanism forms the foundation of many modern AI models such as the Transformer. In one subclass of problems where attention is used, inputs and outputs are bound to the probability simplex so that all outputs sum to one. In this setting, softmax attention admits an exact, component-by-component quantum realization. Attention scores are Hadamard-test statistics on block-encoded projections of amplitude-encoded inputs. The exponential softmax is the interior of a cosine-squared family generated by Born-rule measurement under an exact bijection, whose boundary expresses sparse attention with exact zeros at finite parameter values. The softmax temperature is a repetition count where post-selected measurement rounds realize discretized inverse temperature exactly. Value aggregation is a deterministic column-loading channel that dilates the column-stochastic value matrix. The gated residual is the preparation angle of a single ancilla, with the additive identity at a mixing angle of $\pi$/2. Every learnable parameter is a rotation-gate angle. The composed layer is exact in the infinite-shot limit with one measure-and-reload step per attention score; a fully-coherent variant is $\epsilon$-approximate via quantum singular value transformation in the infinite depth limit. The algebraic core is machine-checked in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Eric A. F. Reinhardt, Adam J. Hauser

item.title: Vanilla Exact Synthesis of CNOT Circuits is NP-hard
item.description: arXiv:2609.04160v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Exact CNOT synthesis seeks a minimum-size circuit implementing a given invertible binary linear transformation. We study its vanilla formulation: synthesis from the identity on fixed labeled qubits, without ancillas and with all-to-all connectivity. We prove that this problem is NP-hard and that its bounded decision version is NP-complete. Hardness persists even for unitriangular targets that are low-rank perturbations of the identity and under near-linear gate budgets. Our proof gives a polynomial-time reduction from the NP-complete Hamiltonian path problem on grid graphs. A unary hypercube embedding translates graph vertices into circuit parities and edge traversals into CNOT updates. The central challenge is that Hamiltonian paths require intermediate vertex visits, whereas exact synthesis constrains only the final transformation. We bridge this gap with a replicated recorder qubits construction that encodes the required parities in the final outputs, together with a tight gate budget that forces every sufficiently short implementation to trace a Hamiltonian path. Crucially, this path structure is enforced by the construction rather than imposed as a restriction on the circuit. The result directly implies NP-hardness for shortest word problem and Cayley-graph distance computation over $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ with elementary transvections as generators, as well as fixed-width sequential XOR program minimization. For CNOT-minimal exact phase polynomial synthesis, it yields NP-hardness with a zero phase polynomial; extending the reduction to grid-graph Hamiltonian cycle problem establishes hardness even when the final linear transformation is the identity. These complementary results show that the linear and phase components each independently suffice for NP-hardness of exact phase polynomial synthesis.
item.dc:creator: Chenjian Li, Ji Guan

item.title: Geometric inflation of deviations challenges neural quantum states in dynamics of quantum Ising models
item.description: arXiv:2609.07645v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural quantum states (NQS) have emerged as a powerful framework for simulating non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated quantum systems, offering scalable variational representations of highly entangled states. Yet, accurate NQS simulations have been found to be surprisingly challenging in some physical regimes of limited complexity. Here, we address paradigmatic quench dynamics of a one-dimensional quantum Ising model as a controlled benchmark. Through supervised state reconstruction we establish substantially tighter empirical upper bounds on the required parameter count than previous estimates, ruling out representational limitations as the key obstruction. Instead, we uncover a geometric inflation of small deviations as a hitherto overlooked challenge for accurate solutions of the infinitesimal time-dependent variational principle (TDVP): the dynamical rotation of the kernel of the quantum geometric tensor (QGT) can suddenly lend physical significance to previously irrelevant parameter deviations. The stability of matrix product state solutions of the same TDVP suggests that the non-linearity of the neural network ansatz is the origin of the sensitivity. These results identify QGT-null-space rotation as a geometric diagnostic of sensitive NQS dynamics and as a concrete target for improving TDVP algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Wladislaw Krinitsin, Jonas B. Rigo, Mohammad Abedi, Markus Schmitt

item.title: Path-Degenerate Quantum Interferometry for Loss Resilience in Gravitational-Wave Detectors
item.description: arXiv:2609.12204v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optical decoherence degrades quantum correlations in squeezed states of light, severely limiting the quantum-nondemolition (QND) sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors. Here, we propose the path-degenerate quantum interferometry scheme that obviates the need for entire optical subsystems---including additional filter cavities, auxiliary parametric amplifiers, and Faraday isolators---thereby drastically reducing spatial mode mismatches while inherently integrating variational output, a long-standing theoretical proposal to further deepen the QND regime. We experimentally demonstrate a core aspect of this scheme, achieving a shot-noise-preserving signal enhancement that directly counteracts the detrimental effects of readout loss. By delivering an improved signal-to-quantum-noise ratio solely through the consolidation and reduction of currently considered optical subsystems, our approach offers a highly optimized route toward enhanced quantum-noise reduction in upcoming LIGO upgrades and next-generation gravitational-wave observatories.
item.dc:creator: Jonas Rittmeyer, Niels Boettner, Farid Khalili, Mikhail Korobko, Roman Schnabel

item.title: Partial Stabilizer Learning under Fixed Commuting Constraints and the Absence of a Copy-Rate Discount
item.description: arXiv:2609.13923v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider an unknown pure stabilizer state of \(n\) qudits with a fixed prime local dimension \(p\), together with prescribed commuting Pauli observables. Rather than learning the whole state, the learner must recover only complementary stabilizers that commute with the prescribed observables, together with their eigenvalues. Once the prescribed measurement is performed, this information and the observed outcome determine the corresponding conditional stabilizer state. We compare the number \(k\) of copies available to the learner with the number \(n\) of qudits and refer to their ratio \(k/n\) as the copy rate. Suppose that the dimension \(m\) of the requested complementary stabilizer subspace satisfies \(m=\beta n+o(n)\) for a fixed \(0<\beta\leq1\). If the copy rate converges to a value below one, the optimal exact recovery probabilities and verification scores converge to zero, both in the worst case and under the uniform prior. Conversely, if the number \(k\) of copies minus the number \(n\) of qudits tends to positive infinity, the entire stabilizer state can be identified with probability tending to one, and the requested complementary information can then be extracted. Thus, restricting the learning target to the stabilizer information needed after the prescribed measurement yields no copy-rate discount.
item.dc:creator: Masahito Hayashi, Yimin Lu

item.title: Transverse momentum as the counter-diabatic generator in bent waveguide couplers
item.description: arXiv:2609.36431v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bending the axis of a mode-evolution coupler suppresses the nonadiabatic coupling between its supermodes, and bent couplers of this kind were recently shown to realize the counter-diabatic (CD) protocol. Here we identify the operator responsible.
